feedback: If the child says 'both ways are the same / both fine' with no mention of fewer counts, put both counts on one number line so the nine-hop crawl and the three-hop version sit side by side; ask which they'd rather do and why.

If the child insists you must start with the 3 because it is written first, show that starting from 9 still lands on 12, and link the saving to the order-doesn't-change-the-total idea they already know.

If the child reliably picks the larger start for new pairs AND explains it (prompt-free, generalising), extend to larger single-digit pairs; if they can only do it when told 'start from 9', keep comparing hop counts until the choice and reason are their own.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting the count-on from the larger addend reaches the same total with far less work, and this is allowed because addition can be done in any order (commutativity).
learnerActions: For 3 + 9, first count on starting from 3 — draw or hop all nine moves across a number line and watch it crawl from 3 to 12.
Now start from 9 instead and count on three — land on 12 in just three hops.
Say what is the same (both reach 12) and what is different (far fewer hops when you start from the larger number).
Answer: why is swapping the order allowed here? Connect to 'the order you add in doesn't change the total.'
Try the same choice for 2 + 8 and 8 + 2: decide which number to start from and explain your choice before you count.
activities.title: Choose your start: count on from the larger addend

feedback: If the child adds 10 by changing the ones digit (writing 47 + 10 as 48) or by counting up in ones, return to the ten-rod / tens column: adding one whole ten changes the tens count. Have them predict the column, then check.
Common error to watch for and correct: treating 47 + 10 as 48. The correct result is 57 — only the tens digit increases by one.

If they predict correctly and explain the reason, keep examples within the two-digit range for now (no crossing into the hundreds); a case that crosses into hundreds can come later, once the tens-digit insight is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: For two-digit numbers that do not cross into the hundreds, adding ten changes only the tens digit (it goes up by one) because ten is one whole ten; place value, not counting in ones, tells you which column moves.
learnerActions: Before adding, predict: when I add 10 to 47, which digit will change and which will stay the same?
Add one ten-rod to a base-ten representation of 47, or move the tens on a place-value / arrow-card setup, and check: the tens change (4→5) and the ones stay the same, giving 57.
Repeat the predict-then-check for 63 + 10, saying which digit changes and why before you do it.
Explain in your own words why adding ten leaves the ones digit alone.
activities.title: Adding ten: predict which digit moves

feedback: If the child says a square is not a rectangle because they have different names or look different, sort by property so the square lands inside the rectangle set, then name the shared structure.
If the child checks four sides and four right angles to justify the relationship, affirm the property-based reasoning and ask them to find another shape that fits both groups.
Note: the card or paper shapes being sorted are thin physical approximations; focus the child on the mathematical shape represented (its sides and right angles), not on the card itself.
activities.intendedInsight: A square is a special rectangle because it has the defining properties of a rectangle (four sides, four right angles); classification should be based on properties, not names or appearance.
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set of shapes into groups by property: all shapes with four sides, and all shapes with four right angles.

Overlap the two groups (e.g. two overlapping hoops): the overlap holds every shape with four sides and four right angles, which is the rectangle set. See that squares land there alongside the other rectangles, because they have both properties.
Answer: what is the same about a square and a rectangle, and what is different?
State why a square counts as a special rectangle, pointing to the shared properties rather than the name or how it looks.
activities.title: Is a square a kind of rectangle?

feedback: If the child applies the swap to subtraction (treats 12 − 4 like 4 − 12), show with objects that you cannot take 12 away from a group of only 4; the order matters for subtraction even though it doesn't for addition.
If the child prefers Maya's way only because '9 is bigger' without mentioning fewer counts or order, prompt them to compare the hop counts and recall why swapping leaves the total unchanged.
activities.intendedInsight: The reorder-to-the-larger strategy depends on commutativity, which holds for addition but not subtraction; a learner who understands the structure can say where it applies and where it breaks.
learnerActions: Discuss the diagnostic situation: To work out 3 + 9, Sam started at 3 and counted on nine more; Maya started at 9 and counted on three more. Both got 12. Is one way better, and why?
Say why Maya's way is better (fewer to count on) AND why swapping is allowed (order of adding doesn't change the total).
Test whether the swap idea has limits: does swapping the order also work for 12 take away 4 — could I do 4 take away 12 instead? Explain why not.
Give the general rule you've found: reordering is safe for addition but not for subtraction.
activities.title: Does the shortcut still work? Bounding the structure
